articles.title: How to build a semantic image search engine with CLIP and Python
articles.excerpt: I have a folder of photos with filenames like 20251230_141957.JPEG and -7972525063673149628.JPEG. If I wanted to find a photograph of someone at the beach, searching for the word “beach” in File Explo…
articles.body: I have a folder of photos with filenames like 20251230_141957.JPEG and -7972525063673149628.JPEG. If I wanted to find a photograph of someone at the beach, searching for the word “beach” in File Explorer would not help unless I had already named or tagged the photo accordingly. I know what the photograph contains, but that information is missing from its filename. Semantic image search lets you use that knowledge as the query. Instead of matching words against filenames, it compares a representation of your description with representations of the images in your collection. You can also supply another photograph as the query when describing what you want in words is difficult. I built a local Python application that supports both approaches.

articles.title: Inside Claude Code's PreCompact and SessionStart Hooks: Deterministic Memory Injection Without RAG Noise
articles.excerpt: Inside Claude Code's PreCompact and SessionStart Hooks: Deterministic Memory Injection Without RAG Noise Most agent memory systems fail for the same reason: they treat every context window problem as…
articles.body: Inside Claude Code's PreCompact and SessionStart Hooks: Deterministic Memory Injection Without RAG Noise Most agent memory systems fail for the same reason: they treat every context window problem as a vector search problem. When an agent starts a session or hits a context compaction boundary, dumping top-k cosine similarity chunks into the prompt introduces stale architectural assumptions, partial code snippets, and high token overhead. In claude-code-memory , we took a different route. Instead of embedding chunks and hoping retrieval ranks the right paragraph, the system uses Claude Code's native lifecycle hooks ( SessionStart , PreCompact , and Stop ) to inject a deterministic, bounded slice of a SQLite-backed bitemporal knowledge graph and AST-compacted source files.

articles.excerpt: Run each trial as its own GPU job, launch them in parallel, and put a spending cap on every trial and on the sweep as a whole. On Nodus, a Sweep runs one Job template for every combination of the valu…
articles.body: Run each trial as its own GPU job, launch them in parallel, and put a spending cap on every trial and on the sweep as a whole. On Nodus, a Sweep runs one Job template for every combination of the values you list, caps the combined spend with maxCostUSD , and reports what each trial cost. Price it as trials x GPU-hours per trial x hourly rate, then cut it with early stopping, which used 36% to 60% of the full compute in our test. This post shows the setup, a small sweep we ran ourselves, and the cost math for sizing a real one. If you are pricing a single training run, start with our LLM training cost calculator instead. articles.title: A ledger proves integrity, not truth
articles.excerpt: A delivery note says 33 pallets. The driver unloaded 32. The note is uploaded, its fingerprint is written to a ledger, and from that moment the record is tamper-evident. So what has the blockchain pro…
articles.body: A delivery note says 33 pallets. The driver unloaded 32. The note is uploaded, its fingerprint is written to a ledger, and from that moment the record is tamper-evident. So what has the blockchain proved? Chapter 6 of my book, One Shared Record , answers with one line: if a driver wrote 33 and unloaded 32, the chain will faithfully preserve 33 for ever. What a fingerprint proves When a document is anchored, a short fingerprint of the file is written to a ledger together with the time. Anyone can later recompute the fingerprint and compare. If they match, the file is unchanged. That settles two questions completely: is this the same file, and did it exist at that moment? Those two answers end a whole family of freight disputes.

articles.title: BM25 vs Semantic Search vs Hybrid RAG: What My Benchmarks Revealed
articles.excerpt: I built a codebase RAG system using BM25, semantic search, reciprocal rank fusion (RRF), and cross-encoder reranking. I expected hybrid search to outperform semantic search alone. It didn't. On my eva…
articles.body: I built a codebase RAG system using BM25, semantic search, reciprocal rank fusion (RRF), and cross-encoder reranking. I expected hybrid search to outperform semantic search alone. It didn't. On my evaluation set, semantic search achieved an MRR@5 of 0.854, while hybrid RRF dropped to 0.692. Adding cross-encoder reranking changed the result. Here's what I tested and what I learned. The Problem Searching a codebase isn't the same as searching ordinary text. A developer might ask: Where does the application check whether a user is logged in? But the relevant implementation could be a function named decode_access_token . BM25 can find exact identifiers. Semantic search can match questions to code with different wording.

articles.title: Flashdate – a drop-in for Python's dateparser, 100x faster
articles.excerpt: dateparser reads dates the way people write them: "March 5, 2024", "le 5 mars 2024", "3 days ago". It is downloaded about 45 million times a month, and it is slow. One ISO date takes it about 670 micr…
articles.body: dateparser reads dates the way people write them: "March 5, 2024", "le 5 mars 2024", "3 days ago". It is downloaded about 45 million times a month, and it is slow. One ISO date takes it about 670 microseconds. A scraper that reads ten million dates spends about two hours on it. flashdate is a modified copy of dateparser with the same API and the same results. It reads common date formats 100 to 250 times faster, and it is still pure Python. Making it fast was the easier half. The harder half was knowing that it still gives the same answer for every string. This article covers both. Why dateparser is slow dateparser does not know the language of a string in advance.

articles.title: Who turned the W upside down? Why Cassiopeia won't sit still
articles.excerpt: The queen in the northern night sky is supposedly one of the easiest constellations to recognize — you just look for a W. Or is that an M?
articles.body: Some constellations are like old friends. You know them well, they're always there, and they never seem to change. A case in point is Cassiopeia, the queen. Its beautiful name comes from Greek mythology — the mother of Andromeda — and its shape is said to represent a queen sitting on a throne. To a stargazer, Cassiopeia is best known as a prominent northern constellation shaped like the letter W. It's easy to find — look north, find five reasonably bright stars making a W, congratulate yourself on finding Cassiopeia and use it to get somewhere more interesting. It's so often a signpost, not a destination. But look north a few hours after dark this month, and you'll notice the W has gone.
